Mount Tiantai is the place where the Great Master Zhiyi dwelt in seclusion to practice the Way and transmit his teachings.

Although my ancestor’s karmic connections for birth, his attainment of the Way, his manifestation of transformative influence, and his entry into parinirvāṇa did not occur on this mountain—primarily because it fulfilled the prophetic record of Dīpaṃkara and simultaneously realized his lifelong aspirations as recorded in the *Biézhuan* (Separate Biography)—the mountain nonetheless corresponds to the Three Terraces (*Sān tái*) above. Thus, it is so named.
It is named Tiantai (Heavenly Terrace); it was also formerly called Nanyue (South Peak), and in common parlance it is also termed "The Heavenly Ladder" (*Tianti*).

As explained in the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), fascicle 1, section 17: "To 'teach' (*jiao*) means to emulate; it also signifies the principle of transforming sentient beings through rationalization. Regarding the teachings, there are both the "ceremonial aspect of transformation" (*huayi*) and the "method of transformation" (*huafa*.
To speak only of the "Four Teachings" is to establish a general title that encompasses both types. The specific text states: "The Eight Teachings combined..."
The two characters "24" are used merely as a marker for the ritual format. Regarding the establishment of the title, I shall no longer rely on the two texts, the *Shiqian* and the *Jinbi*.
"Gao-li" (Koryo) is the name of a country among the Eastern Barbarians; "shamen" (śramaṇa) is the general designation for those of the Śākya clan.
This is translated as "diligent cessation," meaning to diligently practice various virtues and to cease all evils. Furthermore, śramaṇa...
Those who take "Śākya" as their clan name began with Dharma Master Jin'an. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "The four rivers enter the sea and share the same salty taste;
those of the four castes who leave the household life are all called Śākyas. The *Xianxing Lu* establishes a fourfold classification to distinguish them:
first, those who are śramaṇas but not of the Śākya clan—namely, non-Buddhist renunciants; second, those who are of the Śākya clan but not śramaṇas.
Those who are laypeople of the Śākya clan are the first; those who are śramaṇas of the Śākya clan are the second—these are the monastics of the two lands.
Those who are neither of the Śākya clan nor śramaṇas are the third—these are the laity of the two lands.
Master Zhizhe of Tiantai also termed these the "five flavors."
When Emperor Yang resided in his princely estate as the Prince of Jin, he received the precepts from my Grandfather [Zhiyi]. The Master said to the Prince:

"Your Majesty follows the sacred prohibitions with such earnestness that you should be titled 'King of Universal Retention' (Dhāraṇī-rāja). As for me, who transmits the lamp of the Buddha, I should be called 'The Wise One' (Jñānācārya)" (as recorded in detail in the *Biézhuan*).

Regarding the classification of the teachings, Miaole (Zhanran), the foremost of the commentators, stated: "The four teachings of the transformative ritual are the great outline of the classification of the teachings."

The four teachings of the transformative Dharma constitute the framework for explaining the meaning; they are exhaustive, leaving nothing out. Thus, the interpretation and classification of the entire Great Canon of the Buddha’s teachings is complete without omission.

Previously, in this context, I distinguished the *Tiwei* (Purāṇa) as belonging to that [specific] sutra; although it clarifies the precepts and wholesome deeds of humans and devas, it is nonetheless subsumed within the Tripitaka.
This is fully evident in the tenth fascicle of the *Xuánqiān* (Profound Commentary), which states: "[... at the time of the *Avataṃsaka*, following the sutra..."
Regarding the title *The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Great Vaipulya*, it is established through the threefold perfection of person (*pudgala*), dharma, and metaphor (*upamā*).
Furthermore, there are the single and the compound [combinations], making seven ways of establishing a title, as explained in the first fascicle of the *Miaozong* (e.g., "Clouds," "Lotus," etc.).
The Deer Park is also called the Apple Grove and the Immortal Garden; thus it was in the past that the Tathāgata...

Born into a land where he bestowed transformation, his conditions served as the support for his practice (and so forth). *Ahan* is translated as "Incomparable Dharma. The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery), fascicle eleven, states:
"The *Ekottarika Āgama* clarifies the causes and effects of humans and devas; within this, it elucidates the profound meaning of true stillness.

It variously explains the various dhyānas and samādhis, extensively refutes external paths, and generally teaches impermanence, the knowledge of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path" (text).

Regarding the term *vaipulya* (fangdeng): when established as a name based on the practice of the Dharma, it refers to the four teachings spoken together; because it universally benefits the four types of capacities, it is called "equal" (*sama*).

This refers to the *vaipulya* that functions through "harmonizing and rejecting. However, when the *Xingfajing* (Sutra on the Practice of the Dharma) refers to it as a "Vaipulya scripture," it is named according to its underlying principle.

As the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "This is named a Vaipulya scripture because of the equality of principle; it does not refer to the 'mature butter' (*pakvasarpis*) [stage] of harmonizing and rejecting."

The *Vaipulya-śamatha-vipaśyanā* further enters the "Pool of Coolness" by means of four gates: "Direction" (*fang*) refers to the place where one enters, and "Equality" (*deng*) refers to the principle with which one accords.
This is explained in terms of the convergence of practice and principle. The present period of the *Vaipulya* is not either of the latter two types.

*Vimalakīrti* is translated as "Pure Name" (*Jingming*) or "Undefiled Renown" (*Wugoucheng*). The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* (or *Saṃghāṭasūtra*) is the *Brahmaviśeṣacinti-paripṛcchā-sūtra*. *Laṅkāvatāra* is translated as "Inaccessible."

*Lengyan* (Śūraṅgama) is translated as "Mighty Aspect" (*vīra-lakṣaṇa*). *Samādhi* is translated as "Concentration of Rectification," also called "Right Reception" (*samyag-āpatti*). "Jin" (金) refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
"guang" (光) refers to Prajñā; "ming" (明) refers to Liberation (*vimukti*). Lady Śrīmālā was the daughter of King Prasenajit.
*Mahā* is translated as "Great" or "Much. *Prajñā* is translated as "Wisdom. (This is one of the five reasons for not translating *prajñā*, according to the *Yifa shu*). *Mahā-prajñā*...
*Nirvāṇa* is translated as "Great Parinirvāṇa. Regarding the Tathāgata’s forty-nine years of preaching the Dharma, they are collectively categorized into five periods.

The verse says: Twelve years for the *Āgamas*, eight for the *Vaipulya*, Twenty-two years for the discourse on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, Eight years combined for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa*, And the initial seven days for the *Avataṃsaka*. These constitute the distinct five periods; furthermore, there is a general [classification].
The collection of the sūtras into five periods is as explained in the tenth fascicle (26) of the *Myōhōgen* (*Miaofa lianhua jing xuanyi*).
Regarding the "eight teachings" (up to the point where it says): "thereafter, he brings forth the Zang, Tong, Bie, and Yuan [teachings]."
Not coming from a gradual process, but directly teaching the Great [Vehicle] at the very beginning of the temporal sequence, it is therefore called the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*).
Because the intermediate three flavors (*san-wei*) are adjusted in succession to lead those of the Small [Vehicle] toward the Great, it is called the Gradual Teaching (*jian-jiao*).

Through the inconceivable power of a single sound being understood differently by various listeners such that they do not know one another’s perceptions, it is called the Secret Teaching (*mimi-jiao*). By hearing the Small, one realizes the Great; by hearing the Great, one realizes the Small. Thus, one attains [realization].

Furthermore, because their names differ and their teachings are not fixed, the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma contain the Dharma and its meanings in distinct categories; thus they are called the "Threefold Canon" (Tripiṭaka).
These are the common practice of the Three Vehicles, which—because they encompass the Shared, Distinct, and Complete [teachings]—is termed the "Shared Teaching.

It is the unique Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, wherein the stages of sequential severance and realization differ from those of the preceding Canon and Shared [teachings], and precede those of the Distinct and Complete [teachings] regarding wisdom and realization.
The stage of the practice of severance (*prahāṇa-caryā*) is called the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) because all causes and effects are perfectly interfused therein.
Regarding the first, the Sudden Teaching (*dun jiao*): in terms of its teaching, the name is inclusive.

As for the Tathāgata, he came by means of the path of reality (*tathatā-mārga*) to achieve perfect enlightenment; having brought the three delusions to ultimate cessation, he has exhausted the two deaths (*dvividha-maraṇa*).

The eternal extinction of the three delusions is also called the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*): namely, the four stages of dwelling consisting of *darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* delusions, and the one stage of dwelling consisting of *pāṣaṇa-rajas* (dust-like) and *avidyā* (ignorance) delusions.
These are termed "shared dwelling" for *paricchinna-utpāda* (segmented birth and death), while the "expedient" and "true reality" stages are termed *pariṇāma-utpāda* (transformative birth and death).

Regarding the forty-one positions, these refer to the stages of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*): the divisions of the true aspect, namely the stages of *caryā* (practice), *vihāra* (dwelling), *mūrdhan* (peak), *kṣānti* (patience), *bhūmi* (stages), and *saṃbodhi-samantaka* (the stage of near-enlightenment). The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) also states this.
Regarding the forty-one stages in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, although the assembly of bodhisattvas is vast, the stages (*bhūmi*) are cited as a comprehensive framework;
this is like how, though there are many civil and military officials at court, they are collectively referred to as the "hundred ministers.

Those who object on the basis of the text of the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness*—claiming that the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are missing from the beginning and the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samayābhisambodhi*) is missing from the end—are in error, for they are using the discussion of stages within a specific section to challenge the overall structure of the sūtra.

The "multitude" refers to the eight classes: (1) devas, (2) nāgas, (3) yakṣas, (4) gandharvas, (5) asuras, (6) garuḍas, (7) kiṃnaras, and (8) mahoragas; "human and non-human" serves as a summary. One must be likened to the moon:
when the virtue of wisdom gradually becomes full and the darkness of delusion is utterly exhausted, one then achieves the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-dharma*). (And so forth.)
Vairocana is translated as "Pure and Full" (*viśuddha-pūrṇa*) and is also named "Universal Radiance.

He is the teacher of this *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra], who manifested the sublime and extraordinary body beneath the Bodhi tree. *Sūtra* is translated as "Agreement with the Scripture"; it accords with principle and accords with the capacity [of sentient beings].
It is the general name for the twelve divisions [of the canon], yet it is also specifically the first among those twelve divisions. Dragons, ghosts, and others are able to participate in the Dharma.
Because their vehicle is urgent while their precepts are lax, the *Fahua wenju* (Volume 2, Section 23) follows the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in establishing four propositions as usually explained.
This refers to what is said in this sutra: "Like those who are deaf or mute," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the rising of the sun" and so forth, the *Myōgen* (Wondrous Profundity), fascicle one, explains the three illuminations based on the text of the *Ratnagotravibhāga* (Jeweled King Tathāgata-gotra-udaya) from the twenty-ninth chapter of the old translation of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. Therein, there are four points of correspondence and five modes of application;

now, this school combines the four into three and expands the three into five, correlating them with the thirteen noble practices (*ārya-caryā*) and the mutually arising five flavors in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Furthermore, the tenth fascicle of the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) cites the passage from the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra* to correlate it with the five flavors, which are illustrated in the diagram below.
The verse on the twelve divisions of the sūtras states:

The prose (sūtra), the verses (geya), and the predictions (vyākaraṇa); The isolated utterances (udāna), the unasked teachings (nidāna), the causes and conditions (nidāna), the parables (avadāna), and the past events (itivṛttaka);

The birth stories (jātaka), the extensive teachings (vaipulya), the marvelous occurrences (adbhutadharma), and the expositions (upadeśa)—these together constitute the twelvefold division of names. This is explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 37.

The *Miaoxuan* states: "Both the Great and Small Vehicles each possess the twelve divisions [of scripture]. However, within the Small Vehicle, these are explained as not being the meaning of the Great Vehicle; they specifically set aside three and retain nine.

In the Small Vehicle, which is characterized by the cessation of the ashes (nirvāṇa), there are no Vaipulya sūtras. Furthermore, it is taught that [the Buddha] must rely on conditions, and there are no *avaivartika* or *svayambhū* [teachings].
Although there are predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), they record few instances of becoming a Buddha. Thus, one discusses the nine [divisions] of the Great Vehicle and the Small Vehicle."
The eleven sections are explained in detail as conditions in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text), volume sixty-seven.
The "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (*Xìnjiě pǐn*) and the subsequent parables constitute the text that fully summarizes the five periods for the four great disciples;

it employs the expedient means of dispatching attendants to preach the *Huáyán* (Avataṃsaka) teachings to suit their capacities, such as the empowerment of the four bodhisattvas to explain the forty stages of abiding, practice, transference, and realization.
Dharmamati expounds the Ten Abodes; Guṇakara expounds the Ten Practices; Vajradhvaja expounds the Ten Transferences;

and Vajragarbha expounds the Ten Grounds, as detailed in the tenth fascicle of the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning). The śrāvakas sitting in the assembly were like the deaf or the mute:

though they had ears, they did not hear the Perfect and Sudden Teaching; though they had eyes, they did not see the body of Śākyamuni. Because they did not see it, [they failed to perceive the truth].
Because they are unable to offer praise, they are like those who are deaf and mute. This is the same as stated in the first fascicle of the *Miaoxuan*:
"The sudden teaching was originally not intended for those of small capacity; though they may be present in the assembly, they are like the deaf and the mute.

Furthermore, according to the tenth fascicle of the *Miaoxuan*, in the initial section of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* there are never any śrāvakas, whereas in the later sections they do appear. As for the appearance of śrāvakas in the former sections [of other texts], this is a separate tradition.

The *Shuji* (Commentary) states: "By means of what follows, it is revealed that the former [audience] was not yet capable of receiving the Great [Vehicle]" (Text, Vol. 15). Formerly, Huìjué claimed that although the preceding section lacked formal attire, there were those with the *śrāvaka* lineage and nature;
however, this is an error. As for the one who sighed and praised, he was a *śrāvaka*. Thus, it is incorrect.
The second, "Gradual" (śamatha), refers to the teachings on the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and so forth.
Regarding the beginning, middle, and end of this gradual process, it initially suppresses the Great while promoting the Small;

according to the Buddha’s intent, it suppresses [the teaching] at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, while according to the ritual of conversion, it suppresses [the teaching] at the *Avataṃsaka*. It is said that while remaining unmoved in his dwelling, he traveled through bodies and relinquished his precious ornaments.
This is merely to clarify the meaning through these humble writings. Furthermore, that which "travels without moving" refers to wondrous response without deliberation;

though there are differing perceptions regarding its magnitude, it is like people looking at the moon while walking east or west—each has the moon following them, yet the moon itself does not actually go.

Because the *śākyamuni* with his *vairocana*-like majestic marks is adorned with wisdom and meditative concentration, he is compared to a precious ruler; because the *rupakāya* of sixteen cubits endures the afflictions of sentient beings, he manifests in such a manner.

For example, regarding the "worn and soiled" [garments], when the Buddha of sixteen feet in height donned the robes of the two *kṣāntis*, people found it difficult because the robes were sixteen feet long.
This refers to Tuṣita; "reversing contentment" refers to the six heavens of desire and the Brahma world—among these seven heavens, there are inner and outer courtyards where Bodhisattvas reside.
They descend from the inner courtyard to manifest their spirit. Māyā is the Heavenly Queen who transforms and mounts [the elephant].
A white elephant pierced the sun’s orb and entered through the right flank; this was the entrustment of Right Wisdom to the womb.

According to the Mahāyāna, he emerged from the womb riding upon a sandalwood palatial pavilion and other such conveyances. On the eighth day of the fourth month, he descended from his mother’s right flank;

these auspicious signs are fully recorded in the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* (*Lalitavistara*). Regarding his taking of consorts, there were three: first, Gopī; second, Yaśodharā; and third, Mṛgajā. The son born of Yaśodharā was named [Rāhula].
Regarding Rāhula’s renunciation and other events, the verse says:
At nineteen he leaped over the city walls; for six years he practiced austerities. For five years he traveled abroad, and at thirty he attained enlightenment.
He preached the Dharma to save sentient beings for fifty years. Thus, his total lifespan was eighty years.

"Bodhi" is translated as "Way" (Dao). Regarding the "grass seat," the *Sutra on Cause and Effect* (*Hetuphala-sūtra*) states that Śakra transformed himself into the auspicious youth Māṇavaka and offered grass to the Buddha, upon which he sat and attained enlightenment.
The wooden tree and the grass seat both symbolize that the Tripiṭaka explains the nature of arising and ceasing;
thus, the "inferior response" is spoken in contrast to the "superior response" of the Mahāyāna. As for the "five men," the verse says:
Aśvajit, Vāṣpa, and Bhadrika—these three belong to the paternal kin;
Cunda and the Ten-Powered One (Daśabala) belong to the maternal kin. When the Wheel of Dharma was first turned, these were the first to be delivered.
Although various texts present different accounts, I have now illustrated them here to harmonize them.

In the fifth fascicle of the *Wenju* (Commentary on the Words), which corresponds with Master Ying’s *Yiqiejing Yinyi* (Phonetics and Meanings of All Scriptures), Mānava-kulī is identified as the fifth person.
However, the first fascicle of the *Wenju* states that Bāhula is also called Mānava.
I now maintain that "Mānava" translates as "Great Name" (*Mahānāman*) and is likely a general title for the eldest son, whereas Bāhula is [the one who received] the Ambrosia (*Amṛta*).
The *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha* states that Yaśas was the eldest son of King Droṇodana; because he was the eldest son of Droṇodana, both [he and Ājñātakauṇḍinya] could be called Mahānāman.

Otherwise, one fears that the textual passage may have a different source. Although the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Jieshen*) omits Cunda and treats Kauṇḍinya and Mahānāman as two distinct individuals, this must await further investigation; I do not dare to speak of it arbitrarily. This is the truth.

Regarding the passage "The three crossings [are] below; the text clearly explains the matters": the Three Pitakas (Tripitaka) exist as substantial realities that do not immediately coincide with ultimate principle (*tattva*).

Therefore, this section merely demonstrates the historical deeds of the Buddha’s provisional manifestations for the sake of the Hinayana and initial [Mahayana] teachings; it is not a treatise on the eight phases of enlightenment (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*). Nevertheless, concerning the eight phases in both the Great and Small Vehicles, there are differences regarding the subduing of Māra and his existence or non-existence.

According to ancient exegesis, the Great Vehicle lacks the subduing of Māra because the subduing of Māra is understood as the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) itself. Conversely, the Small Vehicle lacks the dwelling in the womb (*garbhasthiti*), as it does not discuss the permanence [of the Buddha].

Because it abides [in the ultimate], we now say that this is not so. In the fifty-eighth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the characteristics of subduing Māra are listed; how could these belong to the Hīnayāna?

Furthermore, since Māra is itself the Dharma-realm, this is possible within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). How should one understand the distinction between the universal and the particular? One should know that the preservation or disappearance of sūtras and śāstras is merely a matter of different explanations according to the capacities of sentient beings.

The eight phases of the minor [Buddhahood] are as described in the *Sìjiàoyì* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings); the eight phases of the major [Buddhahood] are as described in the *Qǐ*... [text fragment].
Regarding the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*: if considered in terms of time, it is like the sun illuminating a dark valley (omitting "until").
It extracts the ninefold *sūtras* from within the twenty-nine fascicles of the older translations of the scriptures, wherein all great mountains and the diamond (*vajra*) jewel mountain are combined.
The reference to the "deep valley" (*yougu*) here, as opposed to the Deer Park (*mṛgadāva*) where the Three Vehicles were first taught, follows the concluding passage of a sutra which states:
"For example, when the sun and moon appear in the world, there is nowhere they do not shine universally, even into deep mountains and secluded valleys" (text).
Regarding the statement that the twelve divisions of scripture produce nine divisions, the intent is to clarify their mutual generation; in reality, the nine divisions also emerge from the Buddha.
The *Śraddhādhimuktiparivarta* states (omitted): "This refers to the meaning of destroying the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as those of views and thought. Regarding the two types of people:

in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), they are the [Four] Truths and the [Twelve] Links of Dependent Origination; in terms of principle (*tattva*), they are the Ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the Conventional (*saṃvṛti*); in terms of persons (*pudgala*), they are the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Because they do not cultivate the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), they are described as "withered and weak"; because they lack fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), they lack majestic power (*tejas*). They proceed slowly...
Regarding "speech," it refers to the phrases and sentences. Because the Great Teaching (Mahāyāna) clarifies the principle of reality, it is said that one "runs swiftly to seize" [the truth].

Because the Lesser Teaching (Hīnayāna) clarifies a principle that is circuitous and obscure, it is said that one "speaks slowly for twenty years. This means that by employing the eight patiences and eight knowledges (*kṣānti-jñāna*) to sever the afflictions of the view-division (*darśana-heya*), these are combined into one non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*) and one liberation (*vimokṣa*).
By employing the nine non-obstructions and nine liberations to sever the afflictions of the cultivation-division (*bhāvanā-heya*), they are collectively perfected.
The twenty [categories] are as explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Wénjù*.
Next, the Vaipulya section is clarified; thus it is said that they "correspond to the teachings.

The Vaipulya accommodates both the Great and the Small vehicles, using the Great to critique the Small and the Perfect to rebuke the Partial. Although all four teachings are expounded therein, [the focus here is on the specific characteristics].
The collection of sutras is very extensive; however, the intent of this treatise is specifically for those of small capacity. The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) states:

"Although it incidentally refutes the Mahāyāna, its primary aim is to refute the Hīnayāna, thereby causing those of small faculties to feel shame for their limited path and to aspire toward the Great. Thus, it is said here that [the Buddha] preached the Perfect [Teaching] in contrast to the Half [Teaching].
As soon as one realizes the small fruit, one is already capable of being rebuked; it is not necessary to wait for twelve years or for subsequent causes.
When Vimalakīrti manifested illness, the Buddha of Vaiśālī commanded his disciples to visit him to inquire after his health;

thus, they all recounted their past experiences of being rebuked by him, their inability to go, the incident of the additional seating arrangement in his room, and the removal of the flowers, as detailed extensively in that sutra.
Regarding the "half" and "full" syllables, the fifth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "For example, it is like an elder who has only one son, and his heart is always..."
Out of affection, [the father] intended to take him to a wise teacher, but fearing he would not achieve success quickly, he brought him back immediately.
Because of his love, he diligently taught him only the "half-syllables" day and night, rather than instructing him in the Vyākaraṇa-śāstra.
This was because his son’s capacity was not yet sufficient; "Vyākaraṇa" translates as "the root of syllables," which is precisely the "full-syllable."
If categorized by time, it is during the mealtime that the mind gradually becomes pure and refined.
"Mealtime" refers to the hour of the *chen* (the third watch). The *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra* explains the four mealtimes: at dawn, the devas eat; at midday, the Buddha eats;
in the afternoon, animals eat; and at dusk, the ghosts and spirits eat. Now, this is the mealtime of the devas. At the hour of the *zi* (midnight), [it is the mealtime of the Buddhas].

The father who trusts [his son] obtains the fruit without fail; the son who trusts his father hears the Great [Vehicle] and does not slander it. Thus they mutually understand one another through faith, which is "compliance.

Hearing the Great [Vehicle] constitutes "entering" and "abiding," while the Small [Vehicle] is named "leaving" one's original place. The thatched hut is a metaphor for the Lesser Nirvana. The Four Clarities (Siming) say:
"Entering the vision of the *Zhuntê* (Exalted Special Body) is due to the function of *karmic consciousness*; because the teaching has not yet been opened, one merely abides in the thatched hut."
Master Yan states that within this assembly, the *Tongjiao* (Common Teaching) is the "request according to the occasion" among the three types of requests;

if one considers the intent of the section, there was no need to conceal it, as it was merely restated for the sake of those who had arrived unexpectedly. Therefore, he previously said: "It accommodates both the Great [Vehicle] and the Small [Vehicle]."
Next, the Prajñā [section] is explained; this is the formal exposition of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
While the meaning shared with the Vaipulya [teachings], which involve refutation and censure, is somewhat remote, this Prajñā section properly belongs to the Shared Division (*gongbu*);

thus, there is both shared *prajñā* and unshared *prajñā*. However, regarding the intent of this division, as stated in the *Fuxing* (The Practice of the Ancients): "It is used peripherally as the Common Teaching (*tongjiao*)."

"By applying the Distinct and Perfect [teachings] to the Two Vehicles, the secret benefit of the Distinct is accomplished" (Text 10, Section 25). Furthermore, the *Shiqian* states: "Since the meaning of the Vaipulya [Vaipulya/Skt.

*vaipulya*] was already established as being common [to all vehicles] previously, when reaching the Prajñā[pāramitā], one need only employ these two [the Distinct and the Perfect] to clarify what is not shared.
This refers to the intent of the [Prajñā] school; although the intent is not shared, there are still those among the newly converted Śrāvakas from the Vaipulya period who reach [this stage].
This "Shared" [teaching] also includes those who have attained a small portion through the "Broad Gate"; therefore, it is employed concurrently (textual passage 33).

Now, as this discussion is conducted by contrasting the partial and the perfect, it is said that while it "bears" both the Shared and the Distinct, it is the Perfect Teaching that is being formally expounded.

As for the four verses on impermanence in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* which resemble the meaning of the Tripitaka, they clarify the auxiliary path and do not represent the primary intent of that division.
In terms of time, it is the hour of *yuzhong* (the "mid-forenoon" period).

Taken as a whole, these are termed "gradual. *Yuzhong* refers to the hour of *si* (10 a.m.–12 p.m.). The term *yu* is also written as *yu* (corner). The "Elder" (*zhǎngzhě*) possesses ten virtues; the Tathāgata possesses the ten titles.

The analogy of gold represents the principles of the Separate Teaching (*biéjiào*), while the analogy of silver represents the principles of the Common Teaching (*tōngjiào*). The clarity of the *prajñā* does not transcend these two.

In the *Prajñā*, the "Perfectly Round" (*yuan*) is also subsumed under the "Distinctive Principle. Regarding the "Precious Treasures," this refers to the exhortation to study, wherein it clarifies the metaphor of the storehouse of all dharma-gates.

As for the extent of what is contained within concentration and wisdom—whether extensive or concise—one should adopt them for one's own practice and bestow them upon others for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
This refers to the Venerable Subhūti; he is also translated as Shanji (Good Auspiciousness) or Shanxian (Good Manifestation), and is foremost among those who understand emptiness.
Śāriputra is the son of one body; he is also translated as "Sparrow-Son" (*Śāriputra*). He is foremost in wisdom, empowered by the Prajñā of emptiness.

Among the two types of persons who turn the wheel of teaching—the Bodhisattvas who bestow empowerment upon those worthy of it—he belongs to the category of those who receive such empowerment. Among the three types of seekers, he corresponds to the seeker of the Dharma.
Regarding the third, the Secret Teaching (*guhyaka-vyākaraṇa*): it is called the "Secret Teaching" because it is [taught] through cessation (*śamatha*).
Because it proceeds in accordance with individual capacities in a concealed manner such that they do not know one another, it is termed "secret.

This differs from the "True Secret" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which is designated as "secret," and from the *Prajñāpāramitā*, wherein the devaputras exclaim: "I see the second dharma in Jambudvīpa."

Regarding the turning of the wheel now, it resembles the initial turning; the Great Commentary (Mahā-śāstra), fascicle 65, explains that the Dharma-wheels of all Buddhas have both manifest and secret aspects.

During the initial turning, the śrāvakas saw eighty thousand devas attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), and Ājñātakauṇḍinya attained the first fruit [of the path]—this is subsumed under the manifest teaching. As for the bodhisattvas, they saw immeasurable asaṃkhyeya beings attain the two vehicles, and immeasurable...

The *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* states that beings attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and so forth (this is a secret teaching). This is explained in detail in the first fascicle of the *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), where it quotes extensively from the twenty-first [section].
Regarding the "three wheels," their meaning is to crush and grind away karma and afflictions; they are also called the "three secrets.

Alternatively, as for the statement that this person is taught the Sudden [Vehicle] and so forth, the first fascicle of the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) indicates that one must manifest signs for a single person or many people in this assembly, based on the ten directions.
One should examine why this is kept secret and how it can be transmitted. As the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) states:

"That which is kept secret and not transmitted is because it is beyond the description of anyone from those below the Buddha; since even Ānanda was unable to receive it, how could it be within the measure of those who propagate the teachings?
Furthermore, it is not that Ānanda did not transmit it; rather, the secrets of the hidden capacities were not what was transmitted. Therefore, it is secret."
That which is used in the Esoteric [Teachings] is entirely the Exoteric Teaching; therefore, the transmission of the Secret is merely called the transmission of the Exoteric (Text 18).
Because its wondrous function covers the capacities [of sentient beings], it cannot be transmitted; once its function has been manifested and described, it can then be transmitted.
The essence of this teaching takes the seven teachings—Sudden and so forth—as its primary substance, and the two principles of True and Middle as its basis.
Regarding the fourth, the "Indeterminate Teaching" (aniyata-deśanā): it is called the Indeterminate Teaching because it is [the teaching of] cessation (*śamatha*).

As for the teaching of a single sound, there is the small and the great; it encompasses both cause and fruit; it includes that which pertains to specific stages (*prādeśika*) and that which transcends them (*atikrānta*);
it includes the manifest and the secret; and it includes the determinate and the indeterminate. Now, this indeterminate single sound encompasses both the small and the great.
Because it is employed by those who have attained the fruit, it causes gradual attainment to yield sudden benefit and sudden attainment to yield gradual benefit;

however, since this benefit is not fixed and belongs solely to the side of the individual's capacity (*mārga*), how can it be called "unfixed teaching"? The teaching is fundamentally intended for the capacity of the individual, and because one obtains benefit through the teaching, all accumulated merit is attributed to the teaching.
Thus, the teaching becomes "unfixed. This arises from the fact that the karmic seeds of past conditions differ among individuals regarding the sudden [vehicle].

There are those who plant seeds gradually and those who plant seeds suddenly within gradual existence; thus, the holy teaching is not fixed in its application. Compared to the previous "secret" [teaching], this is the "manifest" [teaching];
while the application may be indefinite, there is a distinction in the benefits obtained when people with different dispositions encounter the Dharma together and hear it.
The ancient masters pointed to a single sutra or a single passage as the "partial and indefinite teaching," but our school does not hold this view. At one time and in one place...
The first fascicle of the *Vyākhyā on the Indefinite* (*Fǔdìng shìqiàn*) states (22): "In the case of milk, the indefinite is distinguished by correlating it with the Perfect and Distinct [Vehicles].

Although within the teaching concerning curd there is no distinction between two or eight, its meaning can be seen through the correlation of eighty thousand [teachings] with fresh butter and clarified butter, and the three or four [stages] with each other. Thus one knows that... [text ends].
The meditative concentration universally encompasses the four preceding flavors. Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* sometimes speaks of the profound and sometimes speaks of the shallow;

it employs the analogies of "answering what should be questioned by withholding," "withholding what should be answered by questioning," and "the poison that neutralizes poison. These are all characteristics of indeterminate teachings.
This teaching likewise takes the four teachings, such as the *Āgama*, as its essential substance, and takes the two principles of the True and the Middle as its basis.
However, regarding the four teachings of the secret (samatha) method of conversion, they are all equal at this point.

If the first fascicle of the *Fahua xuanji* states that "the secret [teaching] is horizontally bestowed such that there is no time it does not pervade," this is merely said in reference to the Vaipulya (fangdeng) period in contrast to the preceding two periods;

upon examination, this will become clear. Furthermore, [the teachings of] the method of conversion are equal to those of the past, yet they do not extend to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. If one examines the text, the meaning will be seen for oneself.

The *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle ten, states: "Regarding the five flavors, there is a single path that progresses vertically; in each flavor, the provisional (*hān*) and the perfect (*mǎn*) are mutually constitutive.

Furthermore, within each flavor, there are both the secret and the indeterminate [teachings]. (Text, p. 25). This passage discusses mutual constitution by correlating the five flavors with the provisional and the perfect;

therefore, the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning) says: "Although they both travel together (the five flavors and the provisional/perfect are both employed), they alternate between practice and concealment."

The attainment of the "full" (paripūrṇa) as seen in the *Avataṃsaka*—where it is entirely full and not partial—and even the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which sets aside the partial to clarify the full, demonstrates that the partial has the merit of becoming full.
This does not mean that each of the five flavors has its own respective partial and full aspects.

Furthermore, when it is said that "each flavor possesses secret and indeterminate [teachings]," this refers generally to the preceding four periods; it may also imply that the exoteric and esoteric mutually complement one another.
Thus, it is established that what was previously termed "secret" and "indefinite" is now shown in the *Lotus Sūtra* to be "manifest" rather than secret, and "definite" rather than indefinite.
Previously, based on the two commentaries (*Shiguǎn*), difficulties were raised which led to divergent interpretations;

now, I shall directly reveal their underlying intent, so let the reader examine this carefully. As the sixth fascicle of the *Miaoxuan* (fascicle 20) quotes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "Other sūtras are not secret teachings."
The *Huáwéi mìshì qiān* (Secret Commentary on the Profound Meaning), Fascicle Seven (Thirteen), explains: "It is not that 'secret' refers only to the secret [teaching] among the eight teachings;
rather, it is called 'secret' because it has never been spoken before, and it is called 'mysterious' because once it has been opened, there is nothing external to it."
Next, the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*) is discussed. It further states that the three vehicles are merged into the One.

This wondrous Dharma is difficult to understand; thus, it employs the metaphor of the lotus flower. The flower and fruit are simultaneous, and the provisional and the real are one in essence. Furthermore, there are three meanings:

first, for the sake of the lotus, the flower is used as a metaphor for employing the provisional in order to establish the real; second, the opening of the flower and the manifestation of the lotus serve as a metaphor for revealing the provisional.

This reveals the reality through the three flowers falling and the lotus forming as a metaphor for the setting aside of the provisional and the establishment of the real. "Provisional" refers to the four periods and the three teachings; "three" refers to those of the three vehicles.
Now, all are opened and harmonized such that there is nothing that is not the Buddha-vehicle. Furthermore, once opened, there is only the real and no provisional to be discussed;
this meaning corresponds to the "setting aside" [of the provisional]. This is the Trace Gate; furthermore, there is the Root Gate, which sweeps away the traces to reveal the root.

This can be understood through analogies. Furthermore, while the Trace Gate (Jikimon) shares similarities with other sutras, it also possesses differences; though it equally employs the perfect teaching (*en*), it is distinguished by its inclusion of other elements.

The Fundamental Gate (Honmon), however, differs from all other sutras in every respect. While other sutras never speak of a long-established lifespan, there is indeed a profound reason why the Venerable Ancestors have said:
"In principle, it surpasses all sutras; in fact, it excels the entire course of a single transformation."

Regarding the terms "expedient" (quán) and "real" (shí), their names apply to both the ancient and the modern [teachings] (stop). That the name "Exquisite and Unique" (Dúdémiào) is well-deserved indeed has its reason. As for "expedient" and "real":
"expedient" refers to provisional strategies that are used temporarily and then discarded; "real" refers to the precious records that ultimately point to the final destination.

In terms of the expressive language (néngquán), the first three [teachings] are expedient while the Perfect Teaching (Yuánjiào) is real. In terms of what is expressed (suǒquán), they are named True Expedient (Zhēnquán), Middle (Zhōng), and Real (Shí).

Regarding those who comprehend both the ancient and the present: the sutras of the past were indeed subtle in reality but coarse in their provisional means; the sutras of the present reveal that the coarse is itself the subtle.

This meaning is not uniform, as each has its own specific destination; therefore, it is said they are "not the same. At the Deer Park, there was only the coarse, belonging solely to the Tripitaka Teaching (*piṭaka-vinaya*). The *Miao Xuan* states:

"At the Deer Park there were three types of coarseness, while at Vulture Peak there was one type of subtlety. This is spoken in terms of the persons [addressed]; furthermore, it refers to the contrast between the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings (*sādhāraṇa*), and the contrast between the Shared and Distinct Teachings (*pratyekabuddha*).

Regarding the four periods (*catur-yuga*), the ancient schools generally maintained that they encompassed the four propositions—namely, "the old established school," "the school with partial teaching," "the school without [partial] teaching," and so forth—as a means of subsuming the sutras;

however, this is not accepted here. That which alone may be called "wondrous" consists of the wondrousness of relative dependence (*sāpekṣa-pratītyasamutpāda*) and the wondrousness of absolute transcendence (*atyantika-nirapekṣa*).

Because of the revelation and manifestation [of the truth], it differs from the sutras of the past; thus, Miaole (Jingyuan) once said: "The words revealing reality (*bhūta-artha*) universally encompass the opening [of the provisional]."

Question: Regarding this inquiry from the past, if the *Bùyuánjiào* (Teaching of the Perfect Round) does not require further opening (*kāi*), why does the *Miàolè* say that for a person of the Round [Vehicle] at the initial stage, one must hear the "opening and revealing" (*kāixiǎn*) of the true reality (*shíxiàng*) of all phenomena as being separated from the partial? Answer: When one hears the Buddha open up the provisional (*kāquán*) and eliminate the attachment to the partial (*gépiānqíng*), it is not that the Round is being opened;
rather, it is the elimination of such attachments. Furthermore, the *Miàolè* states: "This present sutra is already the Round, yet it still requires opening."
"Manifesting" refers specifically to the perfect [truth] being able to open up the provisional;
thus the text says (omitted): "The marks of the world are eternally abiding" (the principle is one).

Because the provisional is established for the sake of the real, non-duality appears as duality; because the provisional is opened to manifest the real, duality returns to non-duality. Therefore, regarding person and principle...
The four aspects of teaching and practice are all termed "one. First, Guangzhai established the "four ones," namely: one in teaching, one in person, one in cause, and one in fruit.

Our school establishes the "one in practice" to subsume those causes and fruits—meaning the beginning of practice is the cause and the end of practice is the fruit—and adds the "one in principle" to complete the four.
If the one in principle were not clarified, the Dharma would have no point of convergence. The *Wenju*, fascicle 4, states: "There is no duality."
This [teaching] lacks the two [distinctions] of the Half and Full Teachings relative to the Shared Teaching; it lacks the three [vehicles] within the Tripitaka;
furthermore, because it is not accompanied by the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it lacks the two; and because it is not contrasted with the Vaipulya, it lacks the three.
The scripture further states that there is no other vehicle, which refers to the distinct [teaching] of the *Avataṃsaka* and the entry into the distinct via the Perfect [teaching]. This is the Path.

Because it is able to penetrate [reality], it is called "practice" (*caryā*). As for the phrase "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding," these characteristics are identical to the true characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

(And so forth. Since the two phrases beginning with "upright" (*ṛju*) in the sutra are from the text of the Śākyamuni chapter explaining the first [of the three mysteries], they belong to the "teaching" (*śāsana*);
here, however, we take the meaning of the "path" (*mārga*) as "practice."
At that time, because people had not yet attained the wondrous purport of the Lotus Sūtra, they incurred the fault of slander.
In the three cycles of the Trace Gate’s revelation, during the first cycle—the Dharma-exposition—Śāriputra, representing those of superior faculties, receives his prediction;

this section reiterates the provisional teachings of the four periods and brings the three vehicles back to the one vehicle. Next, in the cycle of the Parable, the parables of the three carts and the single cart clarify the meaning.

In the preceding section on the Dharma, the four great disciples were illustrated through the parable of the impoverished son, showing how those of middling faculties attained faith and understanding and would become Buddhas.
In the subsequent section on causes and conditions, it clarifies that the sixteen princes planted the seeds in the interim period of cultivation and now receive their prediction of enlightenment;
this includes the parables of the "transformed city" and the "jeweled destination," whereby those of inferior faculties, such as the twelve hundred śrāvakas and others, attain realization.
Because people do not see his benefits, they bring about slander.
When the time is measured, the solar disc is at its zenith; [therein] the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* emerges.
According to the *Rituals of Zhou*, a one-chi-five-cun earthen gnomon is set up before an eight-foot tall pole; at the summer solstice, at noon, this is used for measurement.

One seeks the center of the earth by means of the sun’s shadow to establish the state. The two masters Yan Guan and Song of the State of Song, together with the Grand Astrologer He Chengtian, employed this method to measure the sun’s shadow to determine the central meridian marker.
To the north, they obtained a shadow of one chi and five cun, equal to the *tugu* (earth-measure ruler).
Since there is one cun of remaining shadow on the ground for every one thousand *li* above the heavens, it was thereby known that [the location] was the center of India.
The term "du" (to cross over) refers to the center of the earth; the current statement that "there is absolutely no side-shadow" is made from the perspective of India.
The original text of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* contains no mention of it "coming forth from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*," but simply states that it "comes forth from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Therefore, the text specifically marks this with two meanings. Now, speaking according to the meaning, it simply says "this comes from," and so forth.

The *Śraddhābhūmi-parivarta* (Chapter on Faith and Understanding) states: "He gathers his kinsmen... [omitted] ...and bestows upon them the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. Here, "kinsmen" refers to the assembly that is the reflection of the Dharma-body.
Both the opening of the teaching and the bestowing of the prediction have both general and specific aspects. The general opening is that all sentient beings shall become Buddhas;
the specific opening is that those who awaken and enter [the path] at this very seat shall attain it. The general prediction is that they shall all attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The *Bodhisattva-vyākaraṇa* records the names of the kalpas, lands, and titles [of Buddhas].
Next, it explains the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* (hereafter abbreviated), which is therefore called the "Gathering Teachings" (*kuṇḍika-śāsana*).
At the beginning of this sutra, the eternal principle is extensively expounded and the Buddha-nature is revealed; it is intended for those of the final age who pursue [the truth].

The exposition of the four teachings (the text from the "Chapter on Holy Conduct") accords with the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra*; the subsequent sublation of the four teachings (from the "Chapter on the Virtuous King") refers to their convergence.
"Sublation" (*mǐn*) means integration. All four [teachings] know the eternal, yet their ultimate intent returns to the perfect reality (*yuan-shi*).

The three provisional teachings are temporarily employed as a respite; in truth, one does not rely on the expedient means as the final goal. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* is likened to the autumn harvest of great reaping, while the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is like the winter storage.
It is like gathering what remains after the harvest.
Second, because the faculties of beings are dull in the final age, it is called the teaching that "supports the Vinaya while discussing the Constant" (扶律談常).
This is a retrospective exposition of the four teachings, which further analyzes the various preceding flavors (*rasa*). Within the sutra, analogies are employed to redeem the present.
The third fascicle of the *Zhongbao Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Treasure Store Treatise), citing a sutra, states:

"For the sake of the bhikṣus of the末法 (final age), they shall possess impure things (the precept-gate of possessing the eight impure things); for the sake of the fourfold assembly, they shall preach that the Tathāgata ultimately enters parinirvāṇa (the vehicle-seed failing to reach the realization of eternal abiding);
and for the sake of extinguishing all evils, they shall preach this sutra. If this sutra perishes, then the Buddha-dharma perishes" (text 26; that passage is more detailed).

Regarding the gains and losses in the discourse on the Dharma-body as the life of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*), because the Vinaya is employed to assist the doctrine of the eternal based on the distinction between delusion and awakening, it is called the "teaching that upholds the Vinaya while discussing the eternal.
