The Master says: As for those who claim that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—both translated by Kumārajīva—use the term "Hīnayāna" as a defining characteristic (*viśeṣaṇa*), since the *Śāstra* already employs the name "Hīnayāna" to refer to the Tripiṭaka teaching, both terms were used together in the translation of the sutra to fulfill the requirements of the verse;
why then must one insist on treating it as a defining characteristic? [Question: Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
The end of the hundred fascicles states: "When the Buddha was in the world, there were no names for the Tripiṭaka;
there were only bhikṣus who maintained the Sūtras, bhikṣus who maintained the Vinaya, and bhikṣus who maintained the Mātṛkā.

(Text) Since the Buddha’s era did not yet have the name "Tripiṭaka," why does the *Lotus Sūtra* speak of "students of the Tripiṭaka"? Zhuan-an replied: "There are differences between earlier and later times."
In the teachings there are the Great and the Small. During the twelve years prior at the Deer Park, he exclusively bestowed the Small Vehicle teachings of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma;
each was maintained independently, and since the Buddha did not designate the Tripiṭaka as "Small," it is said that [the Small] did not exist [as such].

Later, upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which circulate as the definitive scriptures, he criticized the Small and established the Mahāyāna; therefore, the Tripiṭaka is distinguished [as the Small].

Regarding the principle of existence and non-existence in the Hinayana, it can be understood through reflection. Master Huihua said: "In the Buddha's lifetime, the names of the Tripitaka teachings did not not exist;
it was simply that the title 'Tripitaka Dharma Master' did not yet exist. This is the intended meaning of this commentary.
Regarding these three vehicles of spiritual capacity (the section ends here), they generally encompass the cycle of birth and death within the six realms.

As for the equality of the three vehicles: in the teaching of the Four Noble Truths for Śrāvakas, suffering (*duḥkha*) is the primary gateway; in the teaching of Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) for Pratyekabuddhas, origination (*samudaya*) is the primary gateway;

and in the teaching of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) for Bodhisattvas, the path (*mārga*) is the primary gateway. The principles of these eight factors are fully detailed in the *Catuḥsatya-śāstra*.
The Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness (as detailed above): Because they receive the Buddha’s oral teachings, they are called Śrāvakas. Regarding the Four Truths of Arising and Ceasing:

suffering consists of the transition through the three characteristics (arising, changing, and ceasing); origination consists of the movement of the four mental states (greed, hatred, delusion, and their equal proportions);

the path consists of counteractive measures that are subject to change and displacement; and cessation consists of extinguishing existence and returning to non-existence. According to the authentic teachings of the Sage, all four are called "truths" (satya). Furthermore:

Regarding suffering (*duḥkha*), it consists of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) that are impermanent and oppressive; furthermore, three types are discussed: first, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), because it arises from painful sensations (*duḥkhavedanā*);

second, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), because pleasant sensations (*sukhavedanā*) perish; and third, the suffering of formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), because they are constantly shifting and flowing.

The five signs of decay and the eight sufferings are all characteristics of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), for the relationship between cause and effect is never lost. It is briefly said that there are three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), excluding the Brahmā Heaven and the Realm of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*).
The five [heavens] beginning with Avṛha are collectively included within the four types of noble teachings, yet they are specifically categorized into three kinds of existence:
first, to refute the non-Buddhists who reckon Brahmā-king to be the lord who produces all things; second, to refute those who reckon the state of non-perception and mindlessness to be nirvāṇa;
and third, to refute those who reckon the five *anāgāmin* heavens to be true liberation. Thus, the twenty-five royal samādhis refute these twenty [erroneous views].

In the fourth fascicle of the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text), which provides a detailed commentary on the "Chapter on Holy Practice" (*Śrī-vihāra-parivarta*) of the *Pañcavastuka-mahāsūtra*, it discusses the six realms—or as some say, five realms.

The *Fǔxíng* (Sub-commentary), Volume 2, Part 1, page 25, cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, stating that five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the various schools differed in their classifications;
each took passages from the Buddha’s sūtras and interpreted them according to its own tenets. Consequently, there was uncertainty as to whether the realm of Asuras existed as a distinct path or not.

The [textual] accounts differ. Furthermore, the ninth fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* subsumes the asuras within the four destinies (devas, humans, ghosts, and animals), and its commentary also states that the asuras are extracted from the category of ghosts.

Moreover, among the various realms of the six paths of existence, there are none that do not emerge through the four modes of birth—viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, or transformation-born—as stated in the verses of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Humans and animals possess all four modes of birth; those in the hells and the various heavens are born only by transformation.

Intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*) are born only by transformation, while hungry ghosts (*preta*) may be born either from a womb or by transformation. Regarding the six classes of beings who experience desire: their union consists of embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing with lustful intent.
Their development begins like that of a five-day-old embryo up to ten days. Those in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) are fully developed and clothed at birth.
"Those who exist within" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Among those dwelling on earth, sexual union is the means of procreation;

however, for the Trāyastriṃśa gods, it is accomplished through the wind; for the Yāma gods, by embracing; for the Tuṣita gods, by holding hands; for the Nirmāṇarati gods, by laughing; and for the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, merely by looking.

At the beginning of their birth as transformation-born beings, they resemble children of five years of age, up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, who resemble children of ten years of age; thereafter, they gradually grow until the first dhyāna.
At birth, they immediately grow to half a *yojana* in height and are already clad in celestial garments;
although the four modes of birth differ and their bodies and lifespans vary, all beings are subject to birth and death, revolving together in saṃsāra.
First, the hell realm (*niraya-gati*) brings about this bodily existence for that realm.
These hells are located beneath Jambudvīpa and are called the "principal hells" (*maula-naraka*); those between the Cakravāḍa mountains are called the "border hells" (*prādeśika-naraka*).

Jambudvīpa has both principal and border hells; the eastern and western continents have only border hells and no principal ones; and in Uttarakuru, there are neither principal nor border hells. Thus, the northern continent lacks both.

Those who commit transgressions may enter the Southern Barbarians (*nanzheng*) or other peripheral regions. According to the Sanskrit language, because [beings] descend from the Brahma Heaven (*brahmaloka*) birth after birth across kalpas, all the writings of the Kingdom of Chu (India) derive from the Sanskrit.
Thus, when these Sanskrit texts are translated into Chinese, they are termed "translations" (*fanyì*).

In the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou), there is the office of the *xiangxu* (elephant-translators), who communicate the languages of the four directions: those of the East are called *ji*, those of the South are called *xiang*, and those of the West... [text fragmentary].

Fang says that *diti* (pronounced *di*; the word *di* signifies "knowledge") refers to the North, while *yi* refers to the West. Formerly, those who presided over the Western languages were called *diti*, so the two terms combined should be *diti*.

However, all the scriptures use the term *yi*; this is because during the Han dynasty, affairs with the North were frequent, and officials of the Northern Bureau were also proficient in Western languages.
Therefore, it is likely that *yi* is simply a general title for interpreters from all four directions, much like the term used in the Zhou dynasty.

The *Liji* (Book of Rites) states that the officials in charge of foreign affairs were collectively called *xiangxu*. Regarding the eight cold and eight hot hells, they are now summarized here in verse:
*Ābhāsvara*, *Nirarbuda*, With bodies tormented by cold until blisters form and burst, *Atata*, and *Hahava*, And *Huhuva*—these three are all sounds of agony.

Sixth is Utpala-patma (Blue Lotus), eighth is Mahā-patma (Great Red Lotus)—namely, the Blue Lotus, the Red Lotus, and the Great Red Lotus—corresponding respectively to the three types of bodily color [of the hell-dwellers]. (The above are the eight cold hells.

[Preceding these are] Saṃjīva (Reviving), Kālasūtra (Black Rope), and Saṃghāta (Crushing). [In Kālasūtra, beings are first marked with black ropes and then cut and sawed. In Saṃghāta, various instruments of torture arrive and crush them together.

Mutual slaughter; wailing and crying out (the sound of lamentation produced when oppressed by manifold sufferings); loud screaming (the great outcry of resentment when oppressed by extreme suffering).

The six realms of heat (fire follows the body as it turns, making the suffering of heat unbearable). The seventh, extreme cold (whether internally or externally, both one's own body and the bodies of others emit fierce flames that burn and harm one another).

Below these, the eighth is Avīci (alternatively called *Bizi* or *Abisheng*; the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains that in this realm of rebirth, the five factors—time, location, suffering, lifespan, and physical form—are all "without interval").
Each of these eight fundamental hells of cold and heat has its own retinue of countless kinds.

Within each of the eight hells, such as Saṃjīva (Reviving Hell) and the others, there are four gates, and at each gate there are four secondary hells—namely, the Pit of Hot Ashes, the Swamp of Putrid Corpses, the Forest of Razor Blades, and the River of Filth—making sixteen for each primary hell. In total, there are one hundred and twenty.

All eight are called "Increasing Wanderers" (*Utsada*) because the suffering of sentient beings wandering therein increases; the eight cold hells likewise possess one hundred and twenty-eight [subsidiary hells], according to the *Miaoxuan* (Explanations of the Sublime), fascicle six.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* and other texts merely refer to them as "retinues. In the diagrams of the *Abhidharmakośa*, the hot hells are arranged vertically and the cold hells horizontally;
thus, the "Increasing Wanderers" are not listed at the periphery of the eight cold hells. Furthermore, there are the "Solitary" (*Ekākī*) and the "Separated" (*Vivikta*).

Regarding the statement that the hells such as Saṃjīva (Reviving) and others are located throughout the oceans, rivers, mountains, forests, and the air, and endure for kalpas and so forth, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
"The six [hells] beginning with Saṃjīva, in their respective order, have the lifespans of the gods of the desire realm as one day and night. (Human years...)

Fifty years [on earth] constitute one day and night for the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*). Five hundred years of the Four Great Kings constitute one day and night for the Reviving Hell (*Saṃjīva*), which corresponds to nine million years in the human realm. Furthermore, one hundred years in the human realm constitutes one day and night for the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*).

One thousand years of the Heaven of the Thirty-three constitute one day and night for the Black Rope Hell (*Kālasūtra*), which corresponds to thirty-six million years in the human realm (the remaining details are as in the "Chapter on Kalpas" of the Ci'en [Records];

their lifespans are likewise the same). [That is,] the lifespan in the Reviving Hell is the same as five hundred years of the Four Great Kings, and that in the Black Rope Hell is the same as one thousand years of the Heaven of the Thirty-three. Since the lifespan in the Reviving Hell is such, how could it not be so?
[The lifespan] of the Yama hell is half an intermediate kalpa; that of the Extremely Hot (Pratāpana) hell is a full intermediate kalpa;
and for the neighboring hells, it is at most one intermediate kalpa. [As for] the animals, such as the Nanda dragon, their lifespan is one *sthiti-kalpa*.
For the hungry ghosts, it is five hundred years, where one human month constitutes one day; accumulating such days into months, their lifespan is five hundred years. As for the lifespan of Arbuda:
Suppose there were one *bāha* of sesame seeds (a *bāha* is translated as a granary; a granary holds twenty *hu* of sesame, which is the same kind of vessel used nowadays for storing rice).
If someone were to remove a single seed every hundred years until the twenty *hu* were exhausted, that duration is called the lifespan of the Arbuda hell.

Each subsequent hell increases by twenty times this amount (the second, Nirarbuda, has twenty *bāhas* of sesame; the examples for the following six hells may be understood by applying this progressive increase).

Regarding the "upper grade" of the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) and ten evil deeds (*daśākuśala*): those committed with a fierce and sharp mind, without remorse throughout the three periods [of preparation, execution, and completion], are termed "upper grade.

As stated in the *Zhahua chao* (Extracts on Plucking Flowers), etc.: the five heinous crimes are killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an *arhat*, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
The ten evil deeds are: physically, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; verbally, false speech, frivolous chatter, and harsh speech.
The *Sūtra on the Four Liberations* refers to the two types of double-tongued speech, greed, anger, and delusion of the mind as the "Path of Fire.
Second is the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*).

As for the character for this path, it is now mostly pronounced with the sound "chù" (觸). In the *Fuxingji* (Vol. 2, Upper), section 25, it says: "As for 'animals' (*chusheng*), [the character] is *zhǒu* (褚)."

Some permit six directions, while others maintain three; both views are generally accepted. If one uses the pronunciation "chù" (畜), it refers to the six domestic animals—namely oxen, horses, chickens, pigs, dogs, and sheep—and thus fails to encompass all realms of existence (*gati*). However, this discussion of the path is comprehensive and not restricted to these six.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that because their forms are lateral and they move laterally, they are called "lateral beings" (*tiryañc*); alternatively, it is said they are called "pervasive beings" (*tiryag-yoni*) because they exist everywhere throughout the five [realms].
This is because they exist within the Path. Those with much ignorance do not exceed the realm of animals. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* subsumes them under three categories:
those that roam by day, those that roam by night, and those that roam both day and night. Another threefold classification refers to those of water, land, and air.

The *Dīrgha Āgama* explains this extensively (as found in the text). The *Catuḥsmṛty-upadeśa-sūtra* refers to it as the "Path of Blood. As for the middling grade, the mind is somewhat inferior to the former.
Having committed these deeds, one feels little remorse.
Third is the realm of hungry ghosts (end). One receives this physical body of that path.
*Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*), Fascicle 2, Part 1 (25), states: "Cāṭaka" is translated here as "grandfather. According to the *Erya*, the "hun" soul returns [to its source]."
In the *Yeshi zi*, it is said that in antiquity the dead were called "returning persons" (*guiren*).

Furthermore, it states that the spirits of humans are called *gui* (ghosts), the spirits of the earth are called *qi* (earth-deities), and the spirits of heaven are called *ling* (numina). It is also said that those who suffer from hunger are called *egui* (hungry ghosts). They are constantly driven into service;
this realm lies five hundred *yojanas* beneath Jambudvīpa, where the domain of King Yama constitutes its fundamental location.
There are also those who dwell on Jambudvīpa; among them, those with merit dwell in groves of flowering and fruit-bearing trees, while those without merit dwell amidst impurities.
There are likewise hungry ghosts (*preta*) in the two continents of the East and West. In the northern continent (*Uttarakuru*), there are only those possessing majestic power (*vaibhūtika*).

Among the various devas as well, their forms correspond to the places where they are born. [This concludes] the further discussion of the three categories and nine types of internal and external obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), as well as the absence of obstructions.
As explained in the fourth section of the *Ullambana-puṣpa-śāstra*, the *Sūtra on the Fourfold Liberation* refers to the path of knives;

the present *Yankou* (Flaming Mouth) food offering is specifically for the hungry ghosts (*preta*). When making offerings to the *Kāntārī* spirits and the five hundred sons of Hārītī, those of inferior capacity will immediately repent their evil and meager [deeds].

Fourth, the realm of the asuras (cease). Those who have been reborn in this asura body see the devas drinking nectar and gathering flowers from the four continents to brew wine within the great ocean.

Sustained by the karmic power of sentient beings, they advance to seize the nectar but retreat when it fails to become wine; thus, they vow to abstain from it, and so it is said that there is no wine.
Regarding "those who are not handsome": these spirits are sycophantic and crooked; the males are not handsome, while the females are handsome.
Thus, Śacī, the consort of Śakra, is the daughter of Vemacitrin. Regarding "those who are not devas," the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states:
"The word 'a' means 'not'; asura is translated as 'heavenly demon,' for they are not devas. [End of section twenty-five. Some say they engage in battle with the devas.

They are not called "gods" because they do not possess [the status of] devas; those categorized under the realm of ghosts (*preta*) dwell on the shores of the great ocean, while those categorized under the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*) dwell at the bottom of the great ocean.
The rest is as explained in the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary) and the *Wenju* (Explanatory Text). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* clearly elucidates the differences between the four modes of birth:

womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. As for the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*), these are the opposites of the ten unwholesome actions, namely non-killing and so forth, and are here classified as of inferior grade.
The superiority or inferiority of these [rebirths] follows the excellence or deficiency of one's mind; the intermediate cases may be known by analogy.
Fifth, the human path (manuṣya-gati): it brings about this human body.
Humans are the most spiritual among all things; furthermore, humans are the heart of heaven and earth and the vanguard of the five elements (this is according to conventional exegesis).
The *Vibhāṣā* states that among the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), none possess more pride than humans; furthermore, among the five destinies, none are as capable of calming the mind as humans.
Regarding the continents (*dvīpa*), these are dwellings situated within the waters. Here, one should briefly understand the locations of the four continents.
Below are the three wheels: first the wind-circle, then the water-circle, and then the gold-circle. Above the gold-circle are nine mountains and eight seas, and [at their center] is Mount Sumeru.
Mount Cakravāḍa stands at the center, while outside it, surrounding Mount Sumeru, are seven golden mountains and seven seas of fragrant water.

Beyond the seventh mountain is what is called the Earth Circle (*pṛthivī-maṇḍala*), which consists of the four continents. Outside the four continents and within the Iron Encircling Mountains is what is known as the Salt Sea.
This is described in detail in the *Abhidharmakośa*. Pūrvavideha is translated as "Victorious Body" (*vijaya-kāya*); because its physical form is superior, it is so named. Yama... [text truncated]
Jambudvīpa is also called Jambu; by the side of Lake Anavatapta there is a Jambu forest where the trees are tall and large and their fruit is sweet and delicious.

It is named after these trees. Because this [fruit] does not exist in this region, it is not translated [into Chinese]. In the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), it is translated as "Defiled Tree" (*huidu*).
Aparagodānīya is translated as "Ox-Trade. The *Abhidharmakośa-vyākhyā* states that at the beginning of the kalpa, because of its height...
Beneath a tree there was a precious ox used for barter; it was named for this reason. *Uttarakuru* is translated as "Superior Place" (*shengchu*), because it is superior to the three continents.
Regarding the note that the lifespan is one thousand years: only in the Northern Continent is the lifespan fixed at one thousand years;
for the other three, this is stated according to their maximum limit and does not necessarily apply to all cases. As for why sages do not appear within them, it is because... [text ends].
To be born there and manifest transformation is not to say one does not dwell there; according to the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*, Pāṭala, with six hundred followers, dwelt in Uttarakuru.
Regarding the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), they are calculated according to the Dharma. If one discusses retribution (*vipāka*), the Northern Continent is superior to the Southern Continent.
However, if one encounters a Buddha and hears the Dharma, the Southern Continent is superior. The *Mahāvibhāṣā Śāstra* states that even regarding three matters, the Southern Continent is still...
They surpass all the devas, let alone those of the Northern Continent. First, they are able to sever lust; second, they possess the power of mindfulness and awareness;
third, they are capable of diligence. "Constant" means not easily altering one's precepts, thereby preventing what is wrong; "benevolent" means not killing; "righteous" means not stealing;

"ritual" means avoiding sexual misconduct; "trustworthy" means not speaking falsely; and "wise" means not drinking alcohol, for alcohol clouds one's nature. Furthermore, these five precepts constitute four natures.
First, regarding the prohibition [of alcohol]—which restrains other natures that are inherently evil—it serves as the foundation for both major and minor precepts.
Sixth, the heavenly realms consist of the six desire heavens and the twenty-eight form heavens, which differ from one another.
Regarding "Heaven" (*deva*), the worldly interpretation holds that before the primordial qi was differentiated, it existed as a single, undifferentiated whole;
once the two polarities were divided, the clear became Heaven and the turbid became Earth. In the Buddhist scriptures, Heaven is called "Supreme" (*parama*) and also "Radiant" (*prabhāsvara*).
Whether discussing the thirty-three heavens horizontally or the twenty-eight heavens vertically, these refer specifically to the regions above Mount Sumeru. If...

To discuss the scope of the transformation of a single Buddha in general terms, there are three-thousand great thousand-fold world systems (the "three thousands" refer to the small thousand, middle thousand, and great thousand;

these three thousands constitute the totality, while the "great thousand" is the specific unit; by using the specific to manifest the total, the relationship between the whole and its parts is clarified). As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
The four great continents, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, the heavens of the desire realm, and the Brahma worlds—each one thousand of these is called a small chiliocosm.
A thousand times this small chiliocosm is termed a medium chiliocosm;
a thousand times this [medium chiliocosm] is a great trichiliocosm. All of these undergo formation and destruction simultaneously. (Text)

One thousand sets of suns and moons, four continents each, one thousand Sumeru mountains, one thousand heavens of the six desire realms, and one thousand heavens of the first dhyāna are collectively termed a "small thousandfold world-system" (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*).
This is covered by one heaven of the second dhyāna. Furthermore, a small thousandfold world-system is like a single coin;

a medium thousandfold world-system (*dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu*) is like a thousand coins strung together; and a great thousandfold world-system (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*) is like a thousand such thousand-strand bundles. If one were to...

If one hundred thousand is defined as one *koṭi* (億), then there are ten *koṭis* of suns, moons, and Mount Sumerus in a medium-thousandfold world system (*madhyama-sāhasra-lokadhātu*), and ten billion (*daśa-koṭi*) in a great-thousandfold world system (*mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*).

Regarding the statement that there are only "one billion" suns and moons up to "one billion" heavens of the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana, some claim this is an error in the translated text and it should read "ten billion. However, I maintain that there are four types of *koṭi*, the first of which is one hundred thousand.
One hundred million (of the ten billion-fold world systems) makes one *billion*; three thousand million makes one *billion*;
four hundred million makes one *billion*; ten million makes one *billion*. Thus, the "light" refers to the third category [of the ten billion-fold world systems].

Regarding the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, although they are each singular, they are also said to be "ten billion" because one looks down from the higher realms toward the lower. — *Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra* (Ruiying jing).

Regarding the statement that "the center of the three thousand suns and moons and the twelve thousand heavens and earths" refers to the Great Thousand (Mahāsāhasra), the Middle Thousand (Dvisāhasra), and the Small Thousand (Sāhasra):
this means that the place where the Buddha was born is the center of these three thousand worlds.

Furthermore, one must understand that these three thousand worlds share a single cycle of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness; each of these four phases—formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness—consists of twenty periods of increase and decrease.
Regarding the minor and major calamities, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:

"When karma and the paths of unwholesome action increase, the lifespan decreases until [the limit of] ten years, at which point the calamities appear: weapons, disease, and famine respectively (at ten years, weapons;
at twenty, disease; at thirty, famine). They last for seven days, seven months, and seven years respectively (the calamity of weapons lasts for seven..."
[The periods of] seven days and nights, seven months, seven years, seven days and nights, seven months, and seven years and seven days and nights [are the durations of the respective calamities].

Regarding the three calamities of fire, water, and wind, the upper three dhyānas serve as their limits: the second dhyāna is the limit for the calamity of fire, the third dhyāna is the limit for the calamity of water, and the fourth dhyāna is the limit for the calamity of wind.

These correspond respectively to the internal calamities [within those realms]. The fourth [dhyāna] is immovable; therefore, it is not subject to these. This is because the first dhyāna contains vitarka and vicāra (internal discursive thought), which are like fire; the second dhyāna contains... [internal heat].

Because of the presence of the factor of pleasure (*sukha*), the three dhyānas are likened to the calamity of water; because the fourth dhyāna lacks both internal and external factors, it is called "immovable" (*āniñjya*) and is likened to the calamity of wind.

Nevertheless, that receptacle world is not permanent, for it arises and perishes along with the sentient beings who inhabit it (although the palaces of the fourth dhyāna lack such calamities, they perish according to the karmic retribution of the inhabitants).

It requires seven fires followed by one water calamity; after seven cycles of fire and water, there is a wind calamity. After these twenty cycles of increase and decrease, there is finally one fire calamity, similar to this sequence of seven fires.

Furthermore, twenty cycles of increase and decrease constitute one water disaster (*āp-kalpa*). This pattern repeats seven times for fire disasters and once for a water disaster; thereafter, there are another seven fire disasters before a wind disaster (*vāyu-kalpa*) occurs. In total, fifty-six fire disasters, one water disaster, and one wind disaster constitute sixty-four great eons (*mahākalpa*), which is the lifespan in the third dhyāna heaven.

As for the arising of the fire disaster, it is caused by the simultaneous appearance of seven suns. Before the kalpa is destroyed, six of these suns remain hidden within the worlds above and below [Sahāloka].

When the kalpa is destroyed, the remaining six suns gradually emerge. As for the arising of the water disaster, it is caused by the pouring down of torrential rain. As for the arising of the wind disaster, it is caused by the mutual striking of winds; from the lower wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), fierce winds arise due to the power of increasing karma, producing winds in every location. The *Beishan* (Northern Mountain) school states that this is fire.
Calamities rage through the nine heavens, and the whirlwind *vāyu-lavana* sweeps away the third dhyāna; thus, amidst this vast expanse lies the water.
First, the six heavens of the Desire Realm (concluding with) the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
The meaning of the "six desires" is as explained previously. Furthermore, "desire" (kāma) signifies longing or seeking. The six heavens generally possess four types of things:

sentient beings, form, food, and sexual union. Regarding the four heavenly kings: the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east is here called "Holder of the Nation" (Chíguó), for he protects and sustains the land.
He resides on the Golden Mountains and leads two classes of spirits: the Gandharvas and the Kumbhāṇḍas.
In the south is Virūḍhaka (translated as "Increasing"), so called because he causes the roots of goodness in others to increase;
he dwells on Mount Vaiḍūrya and leads two classes of spirits: the Piśācas and the Kumbhāṇḍas.
The king has ninety-one sons, as recorded in the *Linggan zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance). In the west is Virūpākṣa (translated as "Broad Eyes," also known as "Non-...").
He is also called "Good Retribution," "Evil Eye," and "Mixed Speech. Because this king can produce various kinds of speech, he dwells on the White Silver Mountain and leads two classes of spirits:
the poisonous nāgas and the piśācas. In the north is Vaiśravaṇa, which means "Much-Hearing" (Multitudinous Fame);
because he hears much, he dwells on the Crystal Mountain and leads two classes of spirits: the rākṣasas and the yakṣas.
Regarding the establishment of temples for the Heavenly Kings in various locations, this is seen in the first year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty;
as noted in the *Sēngshìlüè*, Sumeru is also called Sumeru, which means "Wondrously Exalted.
It rises eighty-four thousand *yojana*s above the water, and its midpoint is forty-two thousand *yojana*s above the ground. As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
The Sublime High Mountain (Sumeru) has four terraces; The distance between each is ten thousand [yojanas].
Extending outward, they measure sixteen thousand, Eight, four, and two thousand [yojanas] respectively. (This refers to their lateral breadth:
the first terrace is sixteen thousand yojanas wide, the second layer eight thousand, the third layer four thousand, and the fourth layer two thousand.)
Dṛḍhaśiras and Mālādhara, along with the ever-arrogant Great Kings, reside respectively on the four tiers [of Mount Sumeru] (the Four Great Kings), and likewise dwell upon the other seven mountains.
[Dṛḍhapāṇi and the other two are all yakṣa hosts—also called *yakṣas*—who reside respectively on the three lower tiers and also dwell upon the other seven golden mountains;
these are the celestial hosts under the jurisdiction of the Four Great Kings.]

Furthermore, the palaces of the sun and moon are sustained by five winds—namely, (1) Holding, (2) Nourishing, (3) Receiving, (4) Turning, and (5) Adjusting—which encircle their midsections and illuminate the four continents.
The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (meaning "Thirty-three" in Chinese) is situated atop Mount Yugandhara;
at each of the four corners of the summit, there are eight palaces containing the palace of Śakra. In a former age, thirty-three people were made the Heavenly Emperor.
Because the Lord performed supreme deeds in the kingdom of Magadha, they were born together here. The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
"The summit of Sumeru is eighty thousand [yojanas] in diameter; The Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa) dwells there, with four peaks at its corners.
On the four sides dwell the Vajrapāṇis; There are yakṣas named Vajrapāṇi who wield the vajra."
They dwell therein to protect the various devas. The central palace is named Sudarśana (the "Good-to-See," because those who see it praise it as good);

it is ten thousand yojanas in circumference and half a [yojana] in height, with golden walls. Outside the Sudarśana, the city walls are made of gold, one and a half yojanas high, and the city has ten gates.
The ground is variegated and soft; in its center stands the Palace of Excellence (Vaijayanta).
It is one thousand *yojana* in circumference (within the city is a palace, also one thousand *yojana* in circumference).

Outside, it is adorned with four gardens: Saṃtarpaka (Various Chariots), Pāruṣyaka (Coarse and Harsh), Miśravana (Mixed Forest), and Nandana (Joyful Forest). [The first, Saṃtarpaka Garden: Various chariots appear according to the power of the gods' merit. [The second, Pāruṣyaka Garden:

Coarse and harsh weapons of war [such as swords and staves] appear when the gods desire to go to battle. [The third, Miśravana Garden: It is called the Mixed Forest because they experience various sensual pleasures therein. [The fourth, Nandana Garden: It is named the Joyful Forest because it is a realm of supreme excellence that one never tires of beholding.

The Wondrous Grounds (*Sudarśanā bhūmi*) occupy the four cardinal directions, each separated from the others by two thousand [yojanas] (at the edge of each grove there is a ground, separated from the grove by two thousand yojanas).

To the northeast is the Pārijātaka tree (outside the city to the northeast, the tree named Pārijātaka has upright leaves and blooming flowers; its wondrous fragrance is pervasive: with the wind it fills a hundred *yojana*s, and even against the wind it still pervades fifty *yojana*s).
To the southwest is the Sudharmā Hall (where the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven assemble periodically to deliberate on matters of what is in accordance with the Dharma and what is not).
Commentary: Those who practice the ten wholesome actions alone [reside below] Yāma; those above Yāma practice both the wholesome actions and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
*Yāma* is translated as "time-period" (*kāla*), or "virtuous time," because they constantly sing of joy.

*Tuṣita* is translated as "contentment" (*tuṣṭi*), for they give rise to contentment regarding the objects of the five desires. *Nirmāṇarati* refers to those who delight themselves by transforming objects. *Paranirmita-vaśavartin*... [the text continues].

When the gods of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) desire to obtain objects, other gods emanate them for them because they have attained mastery over the use of others' emanations.

Regarding the annotation that this includes those who have attained the "not-yet-reached" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*): when one wishes to be born in those four heavens, one possesses the power of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) itself;

however, those who have not yet reached the fundamental dhyānas (*maula-dhyāna*) are here referred to as having attained the "not-yet-reached" concentration. For now, let it be annotated thus; students should examine this carefully.
Furthermore, among the six *Cūḍika* heavens, there is also the Māra heaven, which is the *devaputra-māra* (the celestial king as Māra) among the four types of Māras.

The *Fahua Wenzhu* (Volume 29) clarifies that the Three Radiant Kings (*Trivikrama-devaputra*) are internal ministers of Śakra, like high officials (*qingxiang*), whereas the Four Heavenly Kings are external ministers, like military generals.
Moreover, Śakra is the lord of the earth-dwelling deities (*bhūmivāsin*), while Māra is the lord of the six heavens of the desire realm (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara*).
Although the Lord [Indra] is the sovereign of the Desire Realm, when he wishes to practice the Buddha-dharma, the Māras cannot restrain him,
as recorded in the *Gantong zhuan*.
Next, the eighteen heavens of the Form Realm are divided into the four dhyānas.
The body of direct retribution (*vipāka*) is a pure form (*rūpa*), not a defiled form stained by the realm of desire.

This follows the Sthavira school’s establishment of eighteen heavens; however, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, only sixteen are established, because the Brahmapurohita and Mahābrahmā are considered one [heaven] as there is no separate location between them, and the Asaṃjñisattva and Bṛhatphala are considered one [heaven] as their lifespan is identical. If it is according to the Sautrāntika school...

The Master [Vasubandhu] further establishes seventeen [levels], because the physical dimensions of the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara devas differ from those of the Brahmakāyika and Mahābrahmā devas.

(The Sautrāntikas—emerging from the Sarvāstivāda at the beginning of the fourth century after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—established their tenets based on the sūtras and did not rely on the vinaya or śāstras. Within the Sthavira school, eighteen levels must be clearly distinguished;

for although the physical dimensions and lifespans of the Bṛhatphala and the Asaṃjñisattvas are the same, their causes and fruits differ. This is because the Bṛhatphala is devoid of vitarka and vicāra.

Regarding the dhyāna of cause and effect where there is no conceptualization because of the absence of mind: the Sanskrit term for *dhyāna* is fully transcribed as *dhyāna*, which translates as "concentration" (*ding*).
Because it involves gathering the mind and focusing it so that it does not scatter, this *dhyāna* serves as the foundation for both mundane and supramundane states.
Each possesses its own branches and subsidiary merits, as detailed in the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm), and so forth.
From the three heavens of the First Dhyāna up to the nine heavens of the Fourth Dhyāna:
"Brahmā" means purity. The Brahmakāyika (Assembly of Brahmā) are the subjects; the Brahmapurohita (Ministers of Brahmā) are the ministers and assistants;

and the Mahābrahmā (Great Brahmā) is the king. When the world is formed, he is the first to be born below; when the kalpa is destroyed, he is the last to perish. Furthermore, there are ten thousand [worlds] within the trichiliocosm.
A hundred million Brahma Kings—only this one is the king within the great trichiliocosm, named Śikhin; he alone attains the status of sovereign over the great trichiliocosm.
None below him can do so, much less govern those above or crown those below. His virtue is most supreme;

his commands are such that even Śakra and the various devas serve as his ministers (as explained in detail in the *Wenju*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra-ṭīkā*). This is clarified in the *Fuxing* (Vol. 13).
Śūrapāla is able to overturn the great trichiliocosm and is honored as a celestial lord, yet he lacks the power of command;

likewise, among the other dhyānas, each takes its superior retribution as its primary characteristic. As for the Parīttābha (Limited Light), because their light is slight within the second dhyāna, they are so named.

As for the Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Light), because their light is infinitely superior, they are so named. As for the Ābhāsvara (Radiant Sound), because they use light as their speech, this is the new translation.

Regarding "Cloudless" (Anabhraka): because the mental consciousness is free from joy and consists purely of the sensation of bliss, the meaning of "Immeasurable Purity" (Apramāṇaśubha) can be understood by analogy with what precedes it.
"Pervasive" (Vibhu) means all-encompassing. As for "Cloudless," those [deities] dwell below in dependence upon space;
because their heads are like dense clouds, they are called "Cloudless. Regarding what the fourth dhyāna depends upon for its abode, the *Karmasūtra* states:
In the fourth dhyāna, the Cloud-Abiding (Megha-vāsī) devas dwell scattered like stars, light and thin, unlike the dense gathering of clouds in the lower heavens.
Those born as "Merit-Born" (Puṇyaprasava) arise in this heaven through the power of having cultivated superior merit; they are so named because their name reflects the cause.

As for the "Vast Fruit" (Bṛhatphala), it is so called because there is no fruit of an ordinary person that surpasses it. As for the "Non-Perception" (Asaṃjñin) devas, during the course of one entire lifespan, the functions of mind and mental factors do not operate.

The Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha), the Heaven of No Heat (Atapa), the Heaven of Good Appearance (Sudṛśa), the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudarśana), and the Heaven of Ultimate Purity (Akaniṣṭha)—these five heavens where the third fruit-dwellers reside are called the Five Non-returner Heavens. According to the sequence in the old diagram of the *Abhidharmakośa*, they are arranged vertically;

however, according to the ninth chapter of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, their locations seem to be horizontal, as shown in the new diagram. Furthermore, within the Heaven of Ultimate Purity, there is the [Vajra] Peak.
Śiva is translated here as Maheśvara (Great Sovereign). These four dhyānas are also called the four samādhis.

In various texts, they are sometimes referred to as the "four dhyānas and eight samādhis," or as the "four dhyānas and four samādhis. Although the four are included within the eight, they are listed separately because they are contrasted with the lower "scattered" (vyavakīrṇa) stages;
thus they are termed "samādhi. Conversely, when contrasted with the higher four samādhis, they are termed "four dhyānas. Thus, their meaning belongs to both categories.

Thus it is. Regarding the four heavens of the three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), these four are also called the four emptiness heavens (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc.). As for the term "formless" (*arūpa*), according to the tenets of the Hīnayāna schools, the Mahāsāṃghika school states: [text continues]

It is simply that coarse form is absent, not that subtle form is absent. The tenet of the *Abhidharmakośa* states that form is non-informative (*avijñapti*) and does not reach the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

However, according to the Mahāyāna, as stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, "The form in the formless realm is not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas" (as cited in the *Fuxingji*, fascicle 6, upper section, line 4).
Examining now the *Shizhuan* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle 3, section 4, it says: "The Hīnayāna asserts its existence."
This is an explanation of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) regarding the formless realms. That which is called the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the Mahāyāna is the opposite of this:
those in the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) grow weary of the physical body and contemplate infinite space, giving rise to the realization of infinite space;

those in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) grow weary of the aforementioned external space and further contemplate internal consciousness, giving rise to the realization of infinite consciousness.

Dwelling in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one becomes weary of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); by contemplating nothingness and realizing nothingness, it is called the sphere of nothingness.

As for "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it is fully termed the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception because there is no perception of the lower stages, yet there is not a total absence of the subtle perception of that stage; thus it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Furthermore, one abandons these two.

One who enters meditative absorption by means of the perception of limits is said to enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the rest is as explained in the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm).
The above explanation establishes that the noble truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) truly exists.
Ordinary beings experience suffering but do not realize it as a Truth; since this is what is elucidated in the initial teaching, it is said that "the Truth of Suffering truly exists.
Second, regarding the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*), it refers merely to the afflictions of the outflows of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-āsrava*).
"Accumulation" (*cita*) has the meaning of "gathering together. Delusion and karma together are capable of gathering together birth and death.
What was previously called the "flowing movement of the four minds" refers precisely to this aggregate of afflictions consisting of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Regarding "view":

if it is said that by seeing the principle one can sever these delusions, then it is named according to its function of liberation; if it is said that "view" itself is provisional, that the provisional is false and inverted, then it is [named] according to its nature as delusion.

Regarding their essential nature, those called "afflictions of attachment" (*tṛṣṇā-kleśa*) are so named because they arise from the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and draw one into the three realms;

these are eliminated upon entering the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), where one repeatedly contemplates the Truth through understanding—this is as explained in detail in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Furthermore, regarding "afflictions of views" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), they arise from mental objects (*dharma-viṣaya*) and are capable of obstructing the True Principle.
Regarding "afflicted ignorance," the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) establishes two types of ignorance. *Miaole* states: "Afflicted ignorance has non-illumination (*avidyā*) as its essence;
non-afflicted ignorance has inferior wisdom (*hīnaprajñā*) as its essence. This refers to [the attachment to] taste, potency, maturation, virtue, time, quantity, and so forth.

As for "pervasive afflictions" (*sāmānyakleśa*), they are common to those of the Three Vehicles; when one cuts through the "sand-grain-like" (*vāluka-saṃkhyeya*) ignorance, they are termed "specific" (*viśeṣa*).
The "branches of delusion" (惑枝末), the "delusions that pervade" (通惑), and the "delusions within the realms" (界內惑)—these three are all designated as such in relation to the Mahāyāna.
The first explanation concerns the delusions of view (見惑), which, when combined, constitute the eighty-eight proclivities (八十八使).

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the clinging to the five aggregates as a self or as a sovereign entity. The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is the clinging to the extremes of annihilation or permanence based upon that view of a self-identity.
The view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is the clinging to what is not *nirvāṇa* as being superior.

The view of grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is taking what is not a true precept to be a precept, such as the practices of chickens, dogs, and so forth. False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is the erroneous mind grasping at principles and denying cause and effect. These are the [five] views.

The dull-witted are always characterized by impulsiveness; that which is called "sharp" arises only through deliberation, while the dull-witted are like those who calculate based on the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*):
they become greedy when praised and angry when reviled, failing to understand this—this is called delusion (*moha*). To treat others with contempt because of this is pride (*māna*).

To be confused and indecisive is the cause for the arising of doubt (*vicikitsā*). These five dull factors are also called "thoughts within views," and "deliberation" (*vitarka*) is also termed [a form of] pride.

The *li-si* (delusion of benefit) is also called the "back-turning messenger" (*bei-shang shi*); since it perishes when the back-turning messenger is eliminated, it is subsumed under the category of views (*dṛṣṭi*).

As previously stated, although these truths reside within karma and afflictions, they are now examined across the four truths. Afflictions are that which cause delusion, while suffering is that which is deluded.
Furthermore, although the Path and Cessation are supramundane causes and effects, because one is deluded regarding Suffering and Origin, one is likewise deluded regarding the Path and Cessation.
It is like being ignorant of the disease and thus deluded regarding the medicine. Regarding these delusions concerning the Four Noble Truths, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
"Under Suffering, all [delusions] are present; In Origin and Cessation, three each are excluded; In the Path, two views are excluded;
In the higher realms, hatred does not occur. (Text)
This involves the distinction between direct and indirect [causality], as explained in the sixty-verse *Gāthā* commentary by Gushan:
"The ten afflictions (*kleśa*) of the Truth of Suffering are all fully present; The view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises solely by taking the object of suffering as its condition.
Ignorance (*moha*), karma, and outflowing causes belong to the Truth of Origination; The unconditioned and outflow-free fruits belong to the Truth of Cessation."
None of these are objects of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—these two do not arise along with it either.

Therefore, by abandoning the three views through the path of accumulation and cessation, the truth of the path fundamentally becomes a cause for the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). For this reason, the view of a self-body does not arise.
Since wrong view denies the existence of the Noble Path, the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) must arise from that wrong view;
by grasping what is not the path as the true path, there is thus the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances.
Regarding the afflictions within the Four Truths, there are those that are distant and those that are proximate: under the truth of suffering, three are distant while seven are proximate.

Grasping at "self" and "what belongs to self" constitutes the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); from this identity-view, one calculates extremes of annihilation or permanence, which is the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
The false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) denies the existence of cause and effect. The grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) consists in clinging to what is inferior as being superior;
the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) consists in regarding what is not a cause as a cause. Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is hesitation and indecision.
Because ignorance is deluded, dark, and lacks understanding, these [seven] all arise based on the object of suffering;

therefore, the seven afflictions are termed "intimate delusions. The three types of afflictions—attachment, aversion, and pride—do not arise from the sphere of the Truth of Suffering, but rather arise by taking the aforementioned seven as their objective support.
Therefore, three [afflictions] are designated as "distant" delusions; The seven, four, and three types are "proximate":
Wrong view, denial, doubt, and hesitation; Adherence to views, attachment to inferiority, and the darkness of ignorance—these three are named "distant" as before.
Greed and the others arise solely based on the four [proximate] factors.
When [the truths] are extinguished, three are direct and four are indirect. Regarding the indirect, the first three are augmented by the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*);
this is the inferior being grasped as superior. Therefore, the grasping at views is established as direct.
Now, the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is a supreme and wondrous dharma; it cannot be further described as inferior being grasped as superior.
Arising solely from the back of wrong view, the grasping of the inferior as superior is called "view-grasping" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
Therefore, regarding the Truth of Cessation, there are four remote [afflictions], while the immediate and remote modes of activity are all as previously stated.
Regarding the Path, eight [afflictions] are present; three are immediate and five are remote. As for the immediate ones, they are delusion, doubt, and wrong view.
Regarding the "abandoned dharmas" (*prahīṇadharma*) compared to the preceding [category], the addition of "prohibiting grasping" (*niyama-parigraha*) is made:

because the precepts and prohibitions of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) serve as causes for tainted results (*sāsravaphala*) rather than untainted paths (*anāsravamārga*), one falsely clings to them as causes and effects;

thus, there exists a direct condition of precepts and prohibitions (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Because the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) is the true cause and the true path, [it is not subject to such clinging].

One cannot take as an object that which is not a cause or a path; since it arises by taking wrong view as its object, the attachment to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is considered a remote factor. Both the path and cessation are untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena;
they are not inferior things held up as superior. The attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is the same as the former and likewise belongs to the category of remote factors.
However, this attachment arises solely from false views; the general explanation based on the *Abhidharmakośa* is as stated above (*Kangenpen*, 35).
Regarding why anger does not function in the two upper realms, the *Abhidharma* states: because there is no mutual harm, because there is wholesome desire, and because their nature [is such].
Because it is tranquil and the mind is moistened, the aforementioned [state] is merely the suppression of [afflictions] so that they do not manifest; it is not their actual eradication.

Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* employs the analogy of centipedes and millipedes to show that anger (*dveṣa*) pervades all three realms. Furthermore, in the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), how could there be the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*)?
Although there is no physical body, there is still the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). Thus, both the sūtras and śāstras state: "The view of self" (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). (See *Fuxing*).

The fifth section below explains the increase and decrease of the ten *anuśayas* (latent proclivities) through the four propositions regarding the *puruṣa* (self). This is based on the Sarvāstivāda school, which maintains that there is also subtle matter (*rūpa*).

As soon as one clings to [this subtle matter] as a sovereign master, it becomes the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). Regarding the "eighty-eight *anuśayas*," this refers only to the afflictions of the category of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states there are "ninety-eight *anuśayas*" because it includes the ten [afflictions] of the category of mental application (*vitarka*). Furthermore, see the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Mohe zhiguan*), fascicle 5.
(Section 10b) By adding the ten *paryavasthānas* (envelopments), they become ninety-eight; these are merely the different enumerations found in the treatises.
Now, I shall further present a diagram of their proximity and remoteness.
Second, regarding the explanation of the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*): [omitted] thus they total eighty-one.
This "thought bound to the realms" (*dhātu-pratisaṃyukta-cetanā*) differs from "simultaneously arising thought" (*sahaja-cetanā*) and "discriminative thought" (*abhisamskārika-cetanā*).
Regarding "the nine stages" (*navabhūmi*): this name is derived from its basis [the nine levels of existence], not because earth, stones, greed, hatred, delusion, or pride each possess nine grades;
it is spoken of collectively here, as the three major grades are further divided into nine.

It is not said that those who have already seen the Path have severed doubt; since this thought is an obstructive matter arising from the five sense objects, it is not severed by passing through the Four Truths.
When severing these delusions, one may either directly take the One True Truth as the object or take any one of the Four Truths as the object accordingly.
Therefore, in the clarity of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are like forty li of water, while the delusions of thought (*citta-kleśa*) are like ten li of water.

However, it is said that such *uṣmagata* (heat) dharmas are dharmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and do not exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

One must know that the person capable of cultivating them belongs to all three realms, yet the *uṣmagata* produced by them arises based on the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the form realm. The *Śāstra-śūci* (Commentary on the Subcommentary), citing the *Píngjiā* (School of Evaluation), states:
"These are entirely dharmas of the form realm; they are dharmas abiding in the stage of meditative concentration" (text). The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* provides an explanation in three senses:

First, regarding the predominance of the number [of factors]: it is said that the contemplation which gives rise to the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) arises from many [factors]. Second, regarding the intermediate state:

while all three realms are capable of giving rise to the stage of Heat, because the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) occupies the middle position, it is said that there are three types of form. Third, regarding the location:
speaking in terms of place, it is easy for the form realm to give rise to Heat, whereas in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is difficult (text).
Next, the clarification of the stages of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*) is divided into three parts: the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), which consists of the four fruits.

First, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*) is called the "path of seeing" (*darśana-mārga*) because it perceives the principle and destroys delusions. Second, from the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin-phala*) onward, one relies on the truth through repeated contemplation to destroy the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*);

this is called the "path of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The fourth fruit, where all delusions are exhausted, is called the "path of no-more-learning. Now, the stage of the first fruit begins from the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

The subsequent mind’s patience with suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and true insight (*vidyā*) regarding the eight truths give rise to eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*), totaling sixteen moments of mind.

According to the *Kāya-mukha* (Gate of the Body), these fifteen moments of mind are termed the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) as the candidate for the first fruit (*prathama-phala-pratipannaka*), while the sixteenth moment is included in the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) as the attainment of the first fruit.
According to the *Xixuan Kongmen* (Gate of Analyzing Profound Emptiness), these sixteen moments of mind are termed the Path of Seeing as the attainment of the first fruit.
Since the fruition belongs to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and because the tenets of various schools differ, there is no need to reconcile them here.

Although our own school primarily employs the "existence-gate" (*astivāda*), the Korean master, wishing to make it easier for beginners to understand, has provisionally followed the "emptiness-gate" (*śūnyatāvāda*) in his commentary. Thus, he identifies the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) as the first fruit. Regarding the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*), the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: [The verse follows: "The sixteen moments are the Path of Seeing; the first fifteen are the Path of Application (*prayogamārga*). Thus, the eight patiences and eight knowledges constitute these sixteen moments.
The first fifteen moments constitute the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), because one sees what has never been seen before.

Immediately after the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), taking the suffering of the desire realm as its object, there arises the "Dharma-forbearance" (*dharmakṣānti*) which is untainted (*anāsrava*). Following that forbearance, there arises the "Knowledge of Suffering" (*duḥkhajñāna*).

Next, taking the suffering of the remaining realms as its object, there arise the "Subsequent Forbearance" (*anvayakṣānti*) and "Subsequent Knowledge" (*anvayajñāna*). This process continues by taking the truths of Origin, Cessation, and the Path as their respective objects.
Each of these two [types] is likewise;
first is the *srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer), also known as the "Noble Stage.

A Stream-enterer is one who enters the stream of the Dharma of the Noble Path. The *Vajraśekhara* says they "enter the stream," or alternatively, it is translated as "flowing against the current" (*pratisrota*).

This is the stream of birth and death. Herein, eighty-eight *anuśayas* (latent proclivities) are abandoned through the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Twenty-eight *anuśayas* are abandoned through the Path of Vision;
the remaining sixty *anuśayas* are abandoned through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). (Text) A former master explained: "There are two types of root-natures (*indriya-gotra*).
If one contemplates the Four Truths equally, the eighty-eight *anuśayas* are abandoned through the Path of Vision; if one does not contemplate the Four Truths equally..."

Regarding those who hold that within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) one only abandons the twenty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) under the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) across the three realms, while the remaining [proclivities] under the other three truths are abandoned through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*):
according to the treatises, those who definitively establish that these are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation are of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*).
The second is the Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner).

Because they will return once more, this fruit involves the abandonment of the first six of the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Between the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and this fruit, one must discuss the *kulaṃkula* (family-to-family);
therefore, we shall first clarify how the afflictions of the desire realm moisten seven further births and deaths, and subsequently explain the general [principles].

Having shown the transcendence of the capacities of the faculties (indriya), I shall now separately explain the meaning of "one who goes from family to family" (kulaṃkula). Because afflictions (kleśa) have coarse and subtle degrees, they are divided into nine grades;

because of the power of the untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna), one passes through seven births. I shall summarize this in verse: The afflictions are divided into nine grades Based on their coarseness and subtlety. By the power of the untainted wisdom, One passes through seven births. I have summarized it thus in verse.
The first category moistens two births; the second, third, and fourth each moisten one; the fifth and sixth together moisten six; and the seventh abandons three categories.

As for why seven births are required, the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states: "Within seven lifetimes, the untainted wisdom matures, like taking medicine..."
The illness is eliminated in seven days according to the Dharma of Sū; it transforms once every seven days, like the *kalala* and other embryonic stages;

it is limited to seven generations according to the Dharma of kinsmen; it travels for seven paces due to the power of the four great elements of the seven-step snake, yet does not reach the eighth pace due to the power of the snake's venom;

One should say that there are three instances of "threefold abandonment" (sāṃvṛtti-prahāṇa) and four instances of "leaping" (vyutkrāntaka). Regarding the sequence of leaping, the *Beifeng* (North Peak) commentary states:

If one has fundamentally abandoned nine grades [of defilements], they are now called "one heading toward the third fruit"; if seven or eight grades, they receive the name of "one who has attained the second fruit";

Regarding the leap-over [attainment] that stops at the fourth grade: the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that next, the abandonment of five grades is called the candidate for the stage of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin-pṛthagjana*);

The middle and final pairs are intended to demonstrate that leaping over and succession are identical in their intermediate stages, for in both cases, they are designated as "twice-born" (*dvija*).

Citing the *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) and its commentary, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the *Mahā-śāstra* enumerates seven types: first, *antarāparinirvāyin*; second, *upapadyaparinirvāyin*;

third, *sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*; fourth, *anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*; fifth, *ūrdhvasrotas* (of the form realm); sixth, *dṛṣṭadharmanirvāyin* (of the desire realm); and seventh, *ārūpyadhātuparinirvāyin*.

The theory of "exclusive regression" (yīxiàng lùn tuì) suggests that only those of dull faculties who have abandoned out-flowing wisdom might regress when encountering adverse conditions; this is now further illustrated.

The theory of "sixfold regression" (liùzhǒng lùn tuì) restricts regression to the fourth fruit (arhatship), whereas the general analysis of the four fruits regarding their susceptibility to regression or non-regression is cited from the *Xuanji* (Analysis of the Profound).
The three schools hold differing views: first, the Sarvāstivādins maintain that one does not fall back from the first fruit (*phala*), but may fall back from the latter three fruits;
second, the Mahāsāṃghikas maintain that one falls back from the first three fruits, but not from the fourth;

third, the Sautrāntika school maintains that one does not fall back from the first and fourth fruits, while there is falling back from the two intermediate fruits (as detailed in their respective texts). Their commentary merely notes that it is difficult to definitively establish [the position] of these three masters; I fear...

Regarding the summary of the formation of disputes and their reconciliation, the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra*), fascicle 9, upper section, paragraph 15, cites the *Saṃghabhedavastu*, stating:
"The regression of an Arhat drags along the regression of the second and third fruits. It is like sand in a well: there are bricks above and below, with only sand in between.
If the upper brick collapses, the sand from top to bottom cannot help but collapse as well. The four fruits are like the bricks above.

The fruit is like sand in the middle; the first fruit is like the bottom [of the vessel] (and so on, until: before the first fruit there is no further fruit. If one were to fall back from it, there would be no place to abide (text).
It is not possible for a noble one to fall back and become an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). This accords with the first teacher.

However, since the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) does not equally contemplate the four truths, as stated in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*: "there are twenty-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)."
The remaining sixty *anuśayas* are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). (First, one abandons the delusions of the lower [realms] regarding suffering within the three realms.

Once the views are exhausted, although the principle of the fruit is not yet perfected—for example, Śāriputra still regressed while at the sixth stage—the wisdom that abandons delusions within the latter three fruits comprises both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) types.
Thus, regarding whether one may regress from the four fruits or not, the assertions of the three masters are all as follows: [insert the three masters' positions here].

The "bond of the unobstructed son" refers to the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*). The "bond of the fruit" refers to the substantial nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as retribution.

Although the body is reduced to ashes and wisdom is extinguished such that nothing remains in ultimate nirvana, when Śāriputra entered extinction, why did Cunda answer the Buddha by saying that the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*) does not perish?
The *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle 10, states: "Uncreated karma (*anabhisaṃskāra-karman*) reaches into future ages."
It is called "non-extinguishing" and "not permanent," yet it is not non-extinguishing (text). There is no agent of action; it is merely the perfuming of merit (and so forth).
Because the Śrāvaka seeks only his own deliverance, he is called "solitary"; having severed the nine grades of desire, he establishes the second and third fruits.

Regarding the contemplation of the upper eight stages, there is only the single stage of the Aśaikṣa. As for śamatha and vipaśyanā, it is said: "Just as a dangerous place has many perils and requires walls and ramparts."

The realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) has many difficulties and many fruits; its nature is to be at rest [only through effort]. (Text 6.7) Therefore, one knows that in the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*), the stages (*bhūmi*) have few difficulties and thus establish only a single fruit.

If this is so, among the seven noble ones (*āryapudgala*), two belong to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)—namely, the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*); two belong to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—namely, the one liberated by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and the one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*);

and two belong to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*)—namely, the one liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) and the one liberated not by time (*asamayavimukta*). Furthermore, the "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) is contrasted with the four fruits and their paths of approach (*pratipannaka*).

Why is this so? Some say that because this stage is adjacent to the state of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*) and is about to sever the delusions of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it is established as a distinct stage, much like the "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyaksambodhi*) found in the Separate and Perfect [Teachings]. Now, I maintain that while the positions established by the proponents of Emptiness and the proponents of Existence may differ, these are merely variations in the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Dharma-gate according to what is appropriate.
The *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) clarifies that the attainment of the Body-Witness (*kāyasākṣin*) refers to the meditative absorption of Cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in its semblance form.

The *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) states that one who has not attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) when speaking in contrast to the actual realization of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path.
This concludes the brief explanation of the stages of the śrāvaka.
